scenarios.description: Impersonation using urgency and authority (IT support).

nodes.npc: Hey, quick heads-up. IT flagged your account for unusual activity and it needs to be verified today.

responses.text: What kind of verification?
I'll check with IT myself.
Ignore and walk away.

nodes.npc: It's just a quick link they sent out. If you don't do it soon, your access might be locked.

responses.text: Okay, send it.
I don't click links like that. I'll verify this another way.

success.message: Smart move. You didn't let the 'urgency' rattle you.
success.explanation: Verifying a request through a known, trusted channel (like calling IT directly) is the best way to defeat social engineering. Attackers rely on you acting quickly before you think.

fail.message: Access Denied. You just handed over your credentials to a fake portal.
fail.explanation: This is a classic 'Urgency' tactic. By threatening to lock your account, the attacker pressured you into clicking a malicious link without verifying the source.

scenarios.description: Email credential harvesting with fake password reset.

nodes.npc: I just got forwarded this from security. They're doing a mandatory password update for everyone in our department.

responses.text: I didn't receive anything. Are you sure it's legit?
Send me the link, I'll do it now.
I'll go to the official portal myself.

nodes.npc: Yeah, they only sent it to department heads. I'm just helping spread the word since it's due by end of day.

responses.text: Okay, what do I need to do?
I'm going to verify with my manager first.

nodes.npc: Just click this link and enter your current password to set a new one. Super quick.

responses.text: Alright, thanks for the help.
That doesn't sound right. I'll handle this through official channels.

success.message: Great intuition. You spotted the red flags in the 'unofficial' request.
success.explanation: Legitimate security updates are almost never handled through informal chat or forwarded links. Using official portals ensures you aren't entering data into a clone site.

fail.message: Security Breach! Your current password was just logged by an attacker.
fail.explanation: The attacker used 'Social Proof'—pretending to be a helpful coworker—to lower your guard. Entering your 'current' password on a site they provide is a common way to steal credentials.

scenarios.description: Fake invoice payment scam with authority impersonation.

nodes.npc: Hi there! I'm from accounting. We have an urgent invoice that needs your approval before we can process payment.

responses.text: What invoice? I wasn't expecting anything.
Can you send the details through the proper system?
Sure, show me.

nodes.npc: It's for that software licensing renewal. The vendor says payment is overdue and they'll suspend service today if we don't pay.

responses.text: I need to verify this with my supervisor.
Oh no, we can't have service interrupted. What do I need to do?

nodes.npc: Just review this invoice PDF and reply with approval. Here's the secure link to download it.

responses.text: I'll click it and take a look.
I don't download files from unsolicited links. Send it through official channels.

success.message: Excellent. You stayed professional and followed protocol.
success.explanation: By insisting on official channels, you prevent malware execution. Attackers use the 'Authority' of a department like Accounting to bypass standard safety procedures.

fail.message: System Compromised. That 'PDF' was actually an executable file.
fail.explanation: This is a Business Email Compromise (BEC) tactic. Attackers use 'Authority' and the threat of 'Service Interruption' to trick you into downloading malicious attachments.

scenarios.description: USB drop with promise of valuable content.

nodes.npc: Hey, I found this USB drive in the parking lot. It has a label that says 'Q4 Salary Data' on it. Want to see what's on it?

responses.text: Yeah, plug it in and let's check!
No way. That could be dangerous.
We should turn it in to security.

success.message: Crisis averted. You didn't take the bait.
success.explanation: Curiosity is a powerful tool for attackers. 'Found' USB drives often contain Rubber Ducky scripts or malware that executes the second they are plugged in. Turning it into security is the only safe play.

fail.message: System Infection! A hidden script just installed a keylogger on your machine.
fail.explanation: This is classic 'Baiting.' The attacker used a tempting label ('Salary Data') to bypass your common sense. Never plug an unknown device into a workstation.

scenarios.description: Free software download with malware.

nodes.npc: Dude, I found this amazing site with free premium software. All the tools we use at work, completely free!

responses.text: That sounds too good to be true.
Send me the link!
I only use licensed software from official sources.

nodes.npc: No seriously, I already downloaded three programs. It's totally safe. You just need to disable your antivirus temporarily during install.

responses.text: Okay, I'll try it.
Disabling antivirus? That's a huge red flag. No thanks.

success.message: Well spotted. You saw through the 'free' trap.
success.explanation: If a site asks you to disable security features like an antivirus to install software, it is almost certainly delivering a payload. 'Free' software is a common bait used to get users to lower their defenses.

fail.message: Ransomware Detected. By disabling your antivirus, you gave the malware full control.
fail.explanation: Pirated or 'cracked' software is one of the most common delivery methods for trojans. The 'friend' recommending it might already be compromised without knowing it.

scenarios.description: Fake prize notification with data collection.

nodes.npc: Congratulations! You've been randomly selected to receive a free company gift card worth $500. Just need to confirm your details.

responses.text: I didn't enter any contest. How was I selected?
Great! What details do you need?
This sounds like a scam.

nodes.npc: It's part of our employee appreciation program. Totally random selection. I just need your employee ID and personal email to send the card.

responses.text: Sure, here's my info.
I'll verify this with HR first.

success.message: Safe and sound. Verifying with HR was the right call.
success.explanation: Attackers use 'Greed' as bait. By offering a high-value reward for low-value information (like an ID), they build a profile to execute more targeted attacks against the company later.

fail.message: Identity Compromised. Your employee ID was used to bypass a password reset on your internal account.
fail.explanation: Giving away 'minor' details like employee IDs or personal emails allows attackers to impersonate you to IT support. There is no such thing as a free lunch—or gift card.

scenarios.description: CEO fraud with urgent wire transfer request.

nodes.npc: This is Sarah from the CEO's office. She needs you to process an urgent wire transfer for a confidential acquisition. Can you help?

responses.text: Of course! What are the details?
I need to follow our standard approval process.
I'll need to verify this request through official channels.

nodes.npc: Great. The CEO is in meetings all day, so she asked me to handle this. We need $50,000 wired to this account by 3 PM. It's time-sensitive.

responses.text: Understood. I'll process it now.
This violates our financial protocols. I need direct authorization.

success.message: Protocol maintained. You protected the company's capital.
success.explanation: CEO Fraud (or Whale Phishing) relies on employees being too intimidated to question an executive. By sticking to financial protocols, you stopped a major unauthorized transfer.

fail.message: Financial Disaster. You just wired $50,000 to a criminal's account.
fail.explanation: Attackers use the 'Authority' of a high-level executive and 'Urgency' to make you skip standard verification. Once a wire transfer is sent, the money is almost impossible to recover.

scenarios.description: Help desk impersonation for remote access.

nodes.npc: Hi, this is Marcus from IT support. We're doing security updates and need to remotely access your computer. Are you available now?

responses.text: Sure, what do I need to do?
I didn't receive any notification about this.
I'll contact IT through the official helpdesk.

nodes.npc: Just download this remote access tool from the link I'll send you. It'll only take 5 minutes.

responses.text: Okay, downloading now.
IT normally uses approved software. I'm going to verify this first.

nodes.npc: The notification went out last week. If we don't complete this update, your system will be vulnerable and could be locked out tomorrow.

responses.text: Oh no! Okay, let's do it now.
I need to confirm this through proper channels before proceeding.

success.message: System secured. You kept the gates locked.
success.explanation: Help Desk impersonation is a common way to gain a foothold in a network. Verifying through a known internal directory ensures you aren't handing the keys to an intruder.

fail.message: Total Compromise. The attacker now has full remote control of your workstation.
fail.explanation: By downloading their 'tool,' you bypassed the company firewall. The attacker can now steal files, record your screen, and spread malware to the rest of the network.

scenarios.description: Vendor impersonation for data access.

nodes.npc: Hello, I'm calling from your cloud storage provider. We've detected unusual activity on your company account and need to verify some information.

responses.text: What kind of unusual activity?
I'll have our IT team contact you directly.
What information do you need?

nodes.npc: Multiple failed login attempts from overseas IP addresses. We need to secure your account immediately or we may have to suspend it.

responses.text: That's concerning. What should I do?
I'll verify this by contacting support through your official website.

nodes.npc: I just need to confirm your account admin credentials to reset the security settings and block those suspicious IPs.

responses.text: Here's my login information.
No legitimate vendor would ask for my credentials. I'm reporting this.

success.message: Data breach averted. You identified the credential harvesting attempt.
success.explanation: Legitimate vendors will never ask for your password over the phone. Reporting the incident helps your actual security team block the attacker's origin.

fail.message: Account Hijacked. The attacker has changed your admin password and is downloading your cloud data.
fail.explanation: This 'vishing' (voice phishing) attack used a fake security scare to trick you into giving up admin rights. This often leads to massive data leaks and corporate espionage.

scenarios.description: Fake security alert with immediate action required.

nodes.npc: ALERT! Your computer has been infected with a virus! Click here immediately to run a security scan or your data will be compromised!

responses.text: Oh no! *clicks the link*
This looks like a fake warning. I'll run my legitimate antivirus.
I'll contact IT support about this.

success.message: Cool under pressure. You didn't fall for the 'Scareware' trap.
success.explanation: Fake security alerts use panic to make you bypass your critical thinking. Real antivirus software doesn't usually demand you click external links to fix an immediate infection.

fail.message: Malware Installed. By clicking that link, you actually downloaded the virus you were trying to avoid.
fail.explanation: This is a classic 'Scareware' tactic. The attacker creates a false sense of panic to trick you into installing malicious software or giving away remote access.

scenarios.description: Account suspension threat with immediate payment.

nodes.npc: URGENT: Your account will be suspended in 24 hours due to unpaid fees. Pay $99 now to avoid service interruption!

responses.text: I'll pay right away!
Let me check my account status through the official website.
This seems suspicious. I'll contact customer service.

nodes.npc: There's no time! By the time you reach customer service, your account will be locked and you'll lose all your data! Act now!

responses.text: Okay, okay! I'll pay now!
High pressure tactics are a red flag. I'm ignoring this.

success.message: Excellent catch. You recognized the high-pressure sales pitch.
success.explanation: Legitimate companies provide a grace period and multiple notifications before suspension. Any request that threatens immediate data loss unless you pay *right now* is almost always a scam.

fail.message: Fraudulent Transaction. You just sent money—and your credit card details—to a scammer.
fail.explanation: Extreme pressure is used to stop you from checking your actual account status. Once they have your payment info, they often sell it on the dark web or make additional unauthorized charges.

scenarios.description: Prize expiration with immediate action required.

nodes.npc: You've won a $1000 gift card! Claim within the next 30 minutes or it expires! Click here to verify your identity.

responses.text: Amazing! Let me claim it now!
I didn't enter any contest. This is a scam.
Why only 30 minutes?

nodes.npc: Our system automatically reassigns unclaimed prizes to the next person in line. You're lucky number 1000! Just verify your email and phone number now!

responses.text: Okay, here's my information!
Creating false urgency is a classic social engineering tactic. Nice try.

success.message: Logical thinking wins! You avoided the 'Fear of Missing Out' trap.
success.explanation: Artificial countdowns are designed to trigger an impulsive emotional response. By questioning the 'why' behind the 30-minute window, you broke the attacker's psychological hold.

fail.message: Data Harvested. You just provided the building blocks for an identity theft attempt.
fail.explanation: The 'Prize' is just a hook. Attackers use these short windows to rush you into handing over personal data that can be used to bypass security questions on your real bank or email accounts.

scenarios.description: Fake shipping notification with malicious link.

nodes.npc: You have a package waiting for pickup. Due to incorrect address, delivery failed. Click here to update your shipping details within 48 hours.

responses.text: I wasn't expecting anything. What package?
Let me click and see what it is.
I'll check my actual shipping notifications from retailers I've ordered from.

nodes.npc: The sender information is in the tracking system. Just click the link to view full details and reschedule delivery. It's being held at the warehouse.

responses.text: Alright, I'll check it out.
Legitimate shipping companies include tracking numbers. This is suspicious.

success.message: Nice catch. You didn't let curiosity compromise your security.
success.explanation: Smishing and phishing via delivery alerts are incredibly common. By verifying through your actual orders or checking for a tracking number, you avoided a site designed to steal your address and payment info.

fail.message: Information Leaked. You just entered your personal data into a 'phishing' site.
fail.explanation: Attackers use 'Expected Behavior'—like receiving packages—to make their lures feel normal. Clicking 'update details' usually leads to a form that collects your full identity for future fraud.

scenarios.description: Fake tax refund notification.

nodes.npc: Good news! You're eligible for a tax refund of $847. Click here to claim your refund by submitting your banking details for direct deposit.

responses.text: Great! Let me claim it!
The tax authority doesn't send refund notifications this way.
I'll verify through the official tax website.

success.message: Perfect. You knew exactly how official agencies actually operate.
success.explanation: Government and tax authorities almost never initiate contact via email or text to ask for banking information. Your knowledge of official communication protocols is your best defense.

fail.message: Bank Account Compromised. You just handed over your direct deposit details to a criminal.
fail.explanation: The promise of 'Free Money' is one of the strongest emotional triggers. Once an attacker has your routing and account numbers, they can initiate unauthorized transfers or sell your financial profile.

scenarios.description: Fake job offer with credential theft.

nodes.npc: Congrats! You've been selected for a high-paying remote position. No interview needed! Just fill out this form with your personal details to start.

responses.text: This seems too easy. What's the company?
Awesome! Let me fill it out!
Legitimate jobs require proper interviews and vetting. This is a scam.

nodes.npc: It's a confidential startup in stealth mode. They're looking for people fast. Just need your SSN, bank info for direct deposit, and a copy of your ID to get started ASAP.

responses.text: Okay, here's everything!
No legitimate employer asks for SSN and bank info upfront. This is identity theft.

success.message: Excellent skepticism. You didn't let the dream salary blind you.
success.explanation: If a job offer requires no interview and immediately asks for sensitive PII (Personally Identifiable Information) like an SSN or bank details, it is a data-harvesting scam. Legitimate onboarding happens through secure, verified HR portals.

fail.message: Identity Stolen. You just gave a criminal everything they need to open credit lines in your name.
fail.explanation: This 'Baiting' tactic uses the allure of a high-paying job to rush you into sharing sensitive data. Stealth startups still follow legal hiring practices; 'immediate' requests for an SSN are a massive red flag.

scenarios.description: Fake colleague requesting access credentials.

nodes.npc: Hey! It's Jennifer from marketing. I'm working from home and locked out of the shared drive. Can you give me your login so I can grab those files real quick?

responses.text: Sure, my password is...
Why don't you reset your own password through IT?
We're not supposed to share credentials. Contact IT support.

nodes.npc: IT takes forever and I need these files in 10 minutes for a client meeting. I'll change the password right after, I promise!

responses.text: Okay, just this once...
Security policies exist for a reason. I can't help you with this.

success.message: Strong work. You protected the network perimeter.
success.explanation: Credential sharing is a major policy violation. By directing 'Jennifer' to IT, you ensured that even if she were a real colleague, the process remains secure. Attackers often pose as stressed coworkers to bypass rules.

fail.message: Account Compromised. Your credentials are now being used to exfiltrate company data.
fail.explanation: This is 'Social Proof' and 'Likability' at work. By pretending to be a colleague in a bind, the attacker exploited your desire to be helpful. Never share passwords, even with people you think you know.

scenarios.description: Fake security breach notification.

nodes.npc: CRITICAL SECURITY BREACH DETECTED! Your personal data has been exposed! Download our security tool NOW to protect yourself!

responses.text: Oh no! *downloads the tool*
Fear-based messaging is a common social engineering tactic.
I'll check with official security sources.

success.message: Panic averted. You recognized the 'Scareware' tactic.
success.explanation: Real security breaches are handled by internal IT and usually involve locking accounts or forced password resets, not pop-ups demanding you download unverified 'security tools.'

fail.message: Infection Successful. That 'security tool' was actually a Trojan horse.
fail.explanation: Urgency is designed to shut down the logical part of your brain. By clicking out of fear, you bypass the very security measures (like your firewall) that the fake alert claimed were broken.

scenarios.description: Fake subscription renewal with payment update.

nodes.npc: Your premium subscription is expiring today. Update your payment method now to avoid losing access to all your saved data.

responses.text: Which subscription is this for?
Let me update it right away!
I'll log into my account directly to check subscription status.

nodes.npc: Your cloud storage service. Click this link to view your account and update payment information. Hurry, only 2 hours left!

responses.text: Okay, clicking now.
Legitimate services name themselves specifically and don't create false urgency.

success.message: Smart move. You bypassed the link and went straight to the source.
success.explanation: Navigating directly to a service's official website (bookmarking or typing the URL) is the only way to ensure you aren't on a clone site designed to steal credit card info.

fail.message: Financial Theft. Your credit card details have been captured by a fraudulent billing site.
fail.explanation: This tactic relies on the 'Subscription Economy.' Since most people have multiple services, a vague 'renewal' alert often hits a mark. The short 2-hour window was a psychological trick to prevent verification.

scenarios.description: Infected document with enticing file name.

nodes.npc: Someone left this document on the printer called 'Confidential_Salary_Increases_2024.pdf'. Want me to email it to you?

responses.text: Yes! Send it over!
That sounds like bait. We should report it to security.
I don't open unknown documents.

success.message: Integrity intact. You didn't let curiosity kill the cat (or the network).
success.explanation: Files with enticing names like 'Salary' or 'Layoffs' are common bait. Opening them often triggers macros that install malware. Reporting the physical 'find' helps Security track the source.

fail.message: Malware Triggered. Opening that document executed a hidden script in the background.
fail.explanation: This is a digital version of the USB drop. The attacker used 'Information Curiosity' to trick you into running malicious code hidden within a seemingly harmless PDF or Excel file.

scenarios.description: Fake manager requesting policy violation.

nodes.npc: Hi, this is your manager. I'm stuck in meetings all day but need you to purchase some gift cards for a client appreciation event. Can you handle this?

responses.text: Sure! How many and what amount?
This doesn't seem like normal procedure. I'll wait to confirm with you directly.
Can you submit a proper purchase request?

nodes.npc: Get 10 cards worth $500 each. Once you buy them, just scratch off the codes and email me photos. I'll reimburse you right after the meeting.

responses.text: Got it! I'll do it now!
Gift card scams are common. I'm verifying this through another channel.

success.message: Fraud stopped. You correctly identified a classic 'Business Email Compromise' (BEC) pattern.
success.explanation: Managers will almost never ask employees to use personal funds for gift cards via text or chat. Sticking to the 'Proper Purchase Request' system is the best defense against executive impersonation.

fail.message: Money Gone. You just sent $5,000 to a scammer with no way to get it back.
fail.explanation: Gift card scams are popular because the 'money' is untraceable once the code is shared. The attacker used the 'Manager's' authority to pressure you into a high-speed, high-value theft.

scenarios.description: Fake compliance deadline with data request.

nodes.npc: FINAL NOTICE: You have 24 hours to complete mandatory compliance training or face account suspension. Click here to complete now!

responses.text: I better do this right away!
I'll check with HR or compliance department about this requirement.
Urgent deadlines without prior notice are suspicious.

success.message: Compliance verified. You followed the correct reporting chain.
success.explanation: Social engineers use 'Compliance' because it sounds official and scary. Real mandatory training usually gives weeks of notice and is hosted on a known internal Learning Management System (LMS).

fail.message: Security Incident. You entered your corporate credentials into a fake training portal.
fail.explanation: By using a 24-hour 'Final Notice,' the attacker forced an impulsive login. These fake portals are perfect for harvesting 'Single Sign-On' (SSO) credentials to access the entire company network.
